title: ThermaSense on-prem PrivateLink & egress orchestration — KV cache & latency tuning
topics: p99 latency tuning and throughput targets
summary: Deep technical runbook for deploying Redwood Private in Thermasense's on-prem VPCs with intermittent egress to cloud services. Discussed PrivateLink vs direct peering, NAT/egress patterns, DNS resolver split-horizon, KV cache warming strategies, batching windows and quantization choices to hit p99 latency SLAs. Agreed next steps: topology diagram, security docs, and a 2-week pilot with synthetic load tests.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-12-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 78 mins | Recording: on
Attendees: Maya Collins (Redwood AE); Ravi Shah (Redwood SE); Priya N (Redwood Solutions); Tom Vargas (Redwood SRE); Lena Ortiz (CTO, Thermasense); Samir Patel (Platform); Dr. Mei Huang (ML); Jordan Park (NetOps); Anya (Security)

Summary: Quick tech sync focused on on-prem PrivateLink stitching and egress patterns for Redwood Private. Goal: define pilot topology that meets 20ms p99 for short-chat inference & 150 req/s sustained with KV-cache enabled.

00:00:03 - Maya: ok uh hi everyone thanks for joining from Redwood side, we wanted to run through a very practical topology and then talk perf tuning, so Ravi will lead on topology and Tom will talk about runtime knobs, sound good?
00:00:15 - Lena: yep, thanks. we're real excited; main ask is we need sub-25ms p99 for our safety thermostat inference loop, and the control plane needs to be air gapped for some regions so Private deployment is needed.
00:00:30 - Ravi: got it. first question, do you plan to host the control plane on a colo or inside your existing on-prem VPCs? and would you allow egress to Redwood control plane via PrivateLink endpoints or do you prefer a NAT egress-only pattern?
00:00:45 - Samir: we were thinking control plane stays in our colo, but compute nodes will be in customer racks and peered via MPLS. we prefer no internet egress for telemetry except to a whitelisted, proxied endpoint. PrivateLink sounds ideal but need to understand hairpin / routing implications.
00:01:05 - Jordan: yes our firewall rules are strict. we can do outbound via egress proxy but TCP long-lived connections are okay. DNS is resolved via internal resolver, split-horizon.
00:01:22 - Ravi: ok that's common. pattern we see is: PrivateLink for control-plane API (mTLS), peered network tunnels for model-serving traffic or local-only routing for on-prem. If egress is required for model downloads/updates or telemetry, use a controlled NAT or egress proxy with SNI-based allowlists.
00:01:40 - Dr. Mei: i have a question on KV cache. our prompts are short, median seq length 48 tokens, but some are 512. How will KV cache warmup work if the sequences vary?
00:01:55 - Tom: good question. KV cache benefits when you have long-running sessions or prefix reuse. For short stateless requests, continuous batching and prefix cache aren't as effective. We can configure a TTL-based KV cache with LRU eviction plus optional sticky sessions on the edge gateway so tokens for similar sessions stay warm. Eviction policy matters — conservative TTL for your 48-token median, but allow spikes.
00:02:20 - Samir: can you quantify the hit-rate improvements?
00:02:25 - Ravi: with prefix reuse and 70% session locality you can see token-level savings of 30–50% and p99 latency drops of ~10ms in our internal tests. real numbers depend on prompt reuse.
00:02:40 - Maya: also, quantization tradeoffs — if you move to 4-bit you'll save memory and get higher batch sizes on the same GPU, but small impacts to quality. For safety-critical thermostat decisions, you might keep float16 or 8-bit quant to be conservative.
00:02:55 - Dr. Mei: we can run evals. we need to ensure no false positives on safety thresholds.
00:03:05 - Jordan: what about DNS split-horizon? our resolver returns private IPs for internal services, but PrivateLink endpoints return special DNS names. Any gotchas?
00:03:15 - Ravi: yes common gotcha: clients sometimes resolve to public IPs if stub resolvers or conditional forwarding isn't configured. Ensure resolvers on the compute nodes point to internal resolver and that your resolver has conditional records for privatelink hostnames. Also check TTLs — long TTLs during failover cause blackholing.
00:03:35 - Anya: security asks — how's key management? we need KMS integration + HSM possibility. audit logs retention?
00:03:45 - Priya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS for key wrapping, and you can integrate with on-prem HSM via KMIP or a cloud KMS proxy. Audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM via syslog or S3-equivalent connector; retention configurable. We'll attach SOC2 docs.
00:04:05 - Lena: perf targets: 20ms p99 for short inference, 150 req/s sustained throughput, and cold-starts must be under 400ms. is that realistic?
00:04:15 - Tom: targetable but depends on model size and batch windows. if you're using a 7B quantized model we often hit 10–18ms p99 in a well-warm cluster with KV-cache and micro-batching. Cold start of a new replica can be 200–600ms depending on model weights on disk and if weights are cold; use pre-warmed pool for critical SLA.
00:04:37 - Samir: what's the overhead of pre-warmed pool in terms of cost and memory?
00:04:42 - Ravi: it's a reserved capacity tradeoff — reserve N GPUs standby; each warm replica consumes GPU memory but saves cold-start latency. For example, one M40-style node holding a quantized 7B might cost X in your capacity accounting; we'll provide sizing guidance.
00:04:58 - Maya: we should plan synthetic load tests that mimic your distribution. Dr. Mei can share token histograms.
00:05:05 - Dr. Mei: will do. also curious about batching windows — we need sub-25ms p99, so long batching windows are not an option. how do you balance batching for cost vs latency?
00:05:18 - Tom: use adaptive batching — we keep a micro-batch window of 2–5ms to coalesce a few concurrent requests. For latency-critical paths we set max_batch=4 and target 1–2ms wait. This pushes throughput lower but preserves p99. For bulk offload, use a separate route with larger batch sizes.
00:05:35 - Jordan: NAT hairpin concern: if control-plane lives in same on-prem but behind NAT, will traffic loop?
00:05:42 - Ravi: hairpinning can happen; recommended pattern: use PrivateLink endpoints with host-based routing so traffic never leaves the VPC to the NAT gateway. If you must use NAT for egress, ensure source/destination checks and route tables are set to avoid asymmetric routing. We can provide example iptables/snippets.
00:06:00 - Samir: ok. also we have intermittent bandwidth to internet, so model downloads should be staged. How do updates work?
00:06:08 - Priya: Redwood Private supports pre-staging model layers via an update artifact server you host internally; control-plane triggers switchover once checksums match. If internet is intermittent, we can do delta downloads and use local cache nodes.
00:06:22 - Maya: let's go through a quick pilot topology sketch — Ravi?
00:06:26 - Ravi: slide: three racks with compute nodes, an internal LB, local DNS resolver, and a PrivateLink endpoint to Redwood control plane in the colo. Edge gateway handles sticky sessions and does TLS termination to the model runtime. Egress proxy handles telemetry to whitelisted S3 endpoints. Route tables: ensure the subnet route for 10.0.200.0/24 -> vpc-peering, default route -> egress-proxy.
00:06:50 - Jordan: can you share concrete route table and Security Group examples?
00:06:54 - Ravi: yes will include in artifact. we'll provide sample iptables, route table entries, and HAProxy snippets for health checking the runtime.
00:07:02 - Dr. Mei: on KV-cache eviction, if we set TTL to 60s will we see thrash if many short unique requests?
00:07:09 - Tom: yes thrash risk. smaller TTL plus LFU eviction helps if you have high cardinality. Also consider application-level session affinity so the same device hits the same runtime for some period.
00:07:20 - Samir: curious about monitoring — how do we observe KV hit-rate and perceived latency?
00:07:24 - Priya: Console will expose per-route token counts, KV hit-rate, batch sizes, and p50/p95/p99. We'll also drop traces into your tracing collector via OpenTelemetry.
00:07:34 - Jordan: firewall logs often strip SNI. we rely on SNI for allowlist. Any recommendation?
00:07:38 - Ravi: if SNI is removed, use client certs or IP allowlist at the egress proxy. mTLS for control-plane is recommended.
00:07:46 - Maya: let's talk numbers — if we aim for 150 req/s with average 48 tokens and token cost 0.6ms per token on your infra, what latency do we expect?
00:07:55 - Tom: roughly, generation latency = model compute + batching wait + network. If model compute per token is 0.6ms and you generate average 48 tokens, compute time ~29ms, but with caching you avoid re-computing prefixes. For short outputs (like classification) you might only need 8 tokens so compute is ~5ms. The p99 depends on worst-case seq lengths and cold starts. So picking a smaller model or quantizing reduces per-token ms.
00:08:20 - Lena: that compute math seems higher than our target. we need to trade model complexity vs latency. Can Redwood host smaller specialized models?
00:08:27 - Maya: yes you can deploy a trimmed model variant e.g., 1–2B distilled model which is much faster. We'll provide model recommendation for your accuracy-vs-latency curve.
00:08:36 - Dr. Mei: let's plan an eval matrix: model variants, quant levels (fp16, int8, 4-bit), batching configs, KV TTLs. We'll run A/B on the pilot.
00:08:46 - Samir: agree. timeline?
00:08:48 - Maya: propose 2-week pilot starting 2028-12-28: week 1 topology & connectivity + staged model deploy, week 2 synthetic tests & evals.
00:08:56 - Jordan: can you provide a pre-flight checklist we can run with our NetOps?
00:09:00 - Ravi: yes: DNS conditional records, route tables, SGs, egress proxy config, mTLS certs, KMS endpoints, and model artifact store endpoints. we'll send as a single PDF.
00:09:10 - Anya: security — please include threat model and audit log flow.
00:09:13 - Priya: will provide checklist including SOC2 artifacts, KMS integration options, and HSM notes.
00:09:20 - Maya: quick recap of decisions: PrivateLink for control-plane, edge gateway in each rack for sticky sessions, egress via proxied NAT for telemetry, pre-warmed replicas for latency SLO, KV-cache with conservative TTL and LFU eviction. agreed?
00:09:33 - Lena: agreed.
00:09:35 - Samir: agreed pending artifact review.
00:09:37 - Maya: ok final operational notes: when you hit pilot we'll instrument a guarded rollback and full tracing so we can correlate degraded p99 to kv-hit or batch-size anomalies. we'll also run a cost mock to show reserved capacity tradeoffs.
00:09:52 - Dr. Mei: one last oddball: we run some models on ARM64 edge boards, does Redwood Private support mixed-arch pools?
00:09:58 - Tom: we can do mixed pools but kernels differ — performance varies. For ARM inference we'd recommend separate pool and model compilation step. we'll note that in the runbook.
00:10:08 - Maya: thanks all. we'll circle back — Ravi will push topology + examples, Maya will send security docs. any final questions?
00:10:15 - Jordan: nothing more.
00:10:17 - Lena: thanks, appreciate the level of detail.
